title: The mother downstream
hookLine: downstream, a childless charioteer and his wife pull a basket from the river and raise the boy as their own
carry: vatsalya: the love that raises a child
tomorrow: what will Karna refuse a stranger?
last: KARMA: EVERY ACT IS A SEED.

cards: Downstream, a man and his wife are by the water. He's Adhiratha, a charioteer, a suta, whose work is driving and caring for the chariots of warriors. She's Radha.
The text tells us they have no child. Floating toward them comes a basket. They pull it to the bank, open it, and find a baby boy, glowing, in armor and earrings.
Yesterday we stood with the mother who let go. Today we stand with the parents who catch.

teach.b: Adhiratha and Radha take the boy home and raise him as their son. There's no long debate in the telling. They had no child, and here is one.
They name him Vasusena, a name tied to the armor and earrings he was born with. Later the world will know him as Karna.
And he's also called Radheya, son of Radha, after the woman who raised him, not the one who bore him.

Years later, offered a throne and a royal family, Karna will say it himself: Radha raised him with love, and Adhiratha is his father. Hindus know this shape of story well, because God himself is given one.
In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna is born to Devaki in a prison, and carried across a river by night to be raised by Yashoda in a village of cowherds.
The songs belong to Yashoda: Yashoda tying him to a grinding mortar for stealing butter, Yashoda looking into his open mouth and seeing the whole universe.
The bhakti tradition even names a way of loving God after her: vatsalya, love like a parent's for a child.
That's why so many Hindu homes keep a small image of baby Krishna, Bal Gopal, and wake him, feed him, and sing him to sleep.

teach.h: THE LOVE THAT RAISES YOU IS HOLY.
teach.b: In Hindu teaching, the love that raises a child is holy. Karna will carry two halves all his life, the loss from upstream and the home from downstream, and the poem keeps the second half right in his name.

how: In many Hindu homes a small image of baby Krishna, Bal Gopal or Laddu Gopal, is woken, fed and sung to like a child: vatsalya, the parent's love the bhakti tradition learned from Yashoda. Karna, too, is often called Radheya, after the mother who raised him.

games.q: a friend who's adopted asks if Hindus think only a birth mother is the 'real' one. by today's stories, what fits?
o: the love that raises you is holy: Karna is Radheya, and Krishna is Yashoda's boy.
only the birth mother counts in Hindu teaching.
neither counts; parents don't matter in Hindu teaching.
games.why: Karna keeps Radha in his name, and Hindus sing Yashoda as Krishna's mother. Devaki is honored too; love made Yashoda a mother.

practice: If you have a little shrine, or a picture of baby Krishna, sit with it the way Yashoda would: notice him, and offer something small, a flower, a sip of water, a line of a song.
If you don't pray, picture someone who took you in when they didn't have to, and remember one specific kindness, the smallest you can find. Let it sit in the chest, without needing words.

wordCard.voice: Karna's abandonment. A basket caught downstream, a charioteer and his wife, and a boy named Vasusena, Radheya, Karna.

orig.note: Sanskrit vātsalya: tender love, like a parent's for a child; in bhakti, loving God the way Yashoda loved Krishna.

carryVoice: Your line: vatsalya, the love that raises a child. Radha's, and Yashoda's. Tomorrow: what will Karna refuse a stranger?
